title: Where Has All The Folk-Rock Gone?
summary: Following pop music — especially at the stratum just below the A-list — sometimes feels like following a neverending dance of musicians' pivots. Artists, looking for a breakthrough and having less insight than ever into how to get one, don't develop linearly so much as trade sounds with one another. They shift toward or away from bedroom pop, '80s pop, acoustic pop, and so forth, and sometimes those pivots sync up well enough to look like a trend. This year, that trend is supposedly country music, which, if you believe the headlines, is steadily changing the charts. But that wasn't quite true the last couple of times we did this, and it still isn't. Sure, a few real-deal, deep-fried country artists like Ella Langley have blown up recently — or at least, with apologies to Kenny Atkinson, they've analytically blown up. A few pop artists, like Post Malone or (temporarily) Beyoncé, have deliberately set out to make real-deal country music of their own. Shaboozey is happy to carve space out

summary: Even speaking to him through a Zoom call, and actually being from the area myself, it’s hard to say I’ve ever met someone more Atlanta than Belly Gang Kushington. Meshed with a husky baritone, his thick Adamsville drawl sounds like he’s got molasses and tobacco slathered through his jaw. If you ask him about his family, he’ll tell you about his ghetto fabulous great-auntie, who loved to read the Bible and cook chicken for their church pastor and others in the neighborhood. Maybe he’ll mention seeing pictures of his cousin, who he calls his mama, going to Freaknik. title: Shred Is Back For The Attack
summary: When the 22-year-old producer Mike Varney founded Shrapnel Records in 1980, it became the first dedicated metal label in the United States, beating Jonny Z’s Megaforce and Brian Slagel’s Metal Blade to market by two years. That’s perhaps a surprising distinction for a label with such a narrow stylistic focus. As the burgeoning thrash and death metal scenes pushed American metal to the bleeding edge of heavy music worldwide, Varney stuck to his guns. Shrapnel was founded to serve “a niche within a niche,” as Varney explained to Guitar World in a 2023 interview: “I wasn’t finding enough heavy rock records, and as a consumer, I was looking for the next guitar hero. As I tried to narrow the scope of my record label, it dawned on me that I could be the guy to discover the best new guitar players of the decade. I didn’t have any competition I knew of, so it seemed like a great niche where I could dig in and do something I loved.” The post Shred Is Back For The Attack appeared first on Stereo
